mainTopic: Aggadic praise of תורה and דברי סופרים: רבא's דרשות, רבי עקיבא and נטילת ידים in prison, and שלמה's enactments and teachings
overview: This amud is a long aggadic section about the value of תורה and especially of דברי סופרים, the laws of the חכמים. It opens with the end of a verse in ירמיהו about good and bad figs, which stand for צדיקים and רשעים, and teaches that both will one day give off a good fragrance. רבא then reads a verse in שיר השירים as praise of pure young men, faithful wives, and כנסת ישראל, which took on extra decrees beyond the Torah's. רב חסדא confirms that 'new and old' means rabbinic law and Torah law. רבא teaches that one must be even more careful with דברי סופרים than with דברי תורה, because breaking them makes a person חייב מיתה. A ברייתא then tells how רבי עקיבא in prison would rather risk dying of thirst than eat without נטילת ידים. Next come teachings praising שלמה, who enacted עירובין and נטילת ידים and gave the תורה 'handles' through his parables. רבא also reads another verse in שיר השירים as Israel showing God its Torah scholars. The amud ends with a verse showing that mounds of הלכות come from every stroke of the letters, and a teaching on 'black as a raven' that finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: Good figs are the righteous, bad figs are the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The verse in ירמיהו about two baskets of figs ends, and the דרשה explains that the good figs are צדיקים גמורים and the bad figs are רשעים גמורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: '...that are first-ripe, and the other basket had very bad figs, so bad they could not be eaten.' The good figs are the completely righteous; the bad figs are the completely wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a verse from ירמיהו about two baskets of figs and explains what each basket stands for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes one basket of excellent figs and one basket of figs too rotten to eat. The דרשה turns this picture into two kinds of people: צדיקים גמורים, who are fully good, and רשעים גמורים, who are fully bad. This sets up the worry in the next step about what happens to the bad 'basket'.

keyTerms.meaning: a basket or pot (the word the verse uses for each basket of figs)
first-ripened fruit, the best and earliest

steps.confusionAlert: This amud begins in the middle of a verse. The first words ('first-ripe... and the other basket') are still the end of the quote from ירמיהו, not the גמרא's own words. The explanation starts at 'תאנים הטובות'.

phrases.english: that are first-ripe, and the other basket
phrases.notes: This finishes the good basket in the פסוק and starts the bad one (ירמיהו 24:2).

phrases.english: had very bad figs
so bad that they could not be eaten.
phrases.notes: End of the verse quotation.

phrases.english: The good figs: these are the completely righteous.
The bad figs: these are the completely wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the verse quotation begun earlier and gives its interpretation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two baskets of figs in ירמיהו stand for צדיקים גמורים (good figs) and רשעים גמורים (bad figs).

steps.title: Are the wicked without any hope?
steps.stepSummary: The דרשה raises a worry: if the wicked are rotten figs that cannot be eaten, maybe their hope is gone forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: And perhaps you will say that their hope is lost and their prospects are over?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a concern that comes out of the previous step. It is setting up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling the wicked 'figs that cannot be eaten' sounds final, as if nothing good could ever come from them. The phrase 'ושמא תאמר' brings up this conclusion only so that it can be rejected in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: and perhaps you will say (introduces a mistaken idea that will be corrected)
their prospect, their expectation of a good future

phrases.english: And perhaps you will say
that their hope is lost and their prospect is void?
phrases.notes: Refers to the רשעים, the bad figs.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָם וּבָטַל סִיכּוּיָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a possible but mistaken conclusion from the image of inedible figs in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the רשעים, described as rotten figs, have lost all hope of a good future.

steps.title: Both groups will one day give off fragrance
steps.stepSummary: A verse from שיר השירים, 'הדודאים נתנו ריח,' teaches that both the righteous and the wicked will eventually give off a good fragrance.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse teaches: 'The baskets give off fragrance.' Both these and those will in the future give off fragrance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry with a verse showing that even the wicked still have hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word דודאים (usually 'mandrakes') is read as the plural of דוד, 'basket.' So 'the baskets give off fragrance' refers to both baskets of figs. That means the bad basket, the רשעים, will also give off a pleasant scent in the future, so their hope is not lost.

keyTerms.meaning: the verse teaches (introduces a verse that proves the point)
mandrakes; read here as 'baskets,' the plural of דוּד

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic aggadic idea: even a person who is a רשע גמור is never completely written off. Both groups end up 'fragrant.'

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
'The baskets [duda'im] give off fragrance'
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 7:14. דודאים is read as the plural of דוד, 'basket.'

phrases.english: both these and those will in the future give off fragrance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers and rejects the worry raised in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wicked have not lost hope. 'הדודאים נתנו ריח' shows that both baskets, the righteous and the wicked, will eventually give off fragrance.

steps.title: רבא: the fragrant mandrakes are young men who never sinned
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains 'הדודאים נתנו ריח' differently: the fragrant mandrakes are young Jewish men who never tasted sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא expounded: What is the meaning of the verse, 'The mandrakes give off fragrance'? These are the young men of Israel who have not tasted the taste of sin.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers his own explanation of the same verse from שיר השירים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous step, דודאים meant 'baskets' and referred to both righteous and wicked. רבא reads דודאים as actual fragrant plants, an image of purity, and applies it to young men who have stayed free of sin. It is a separate דרשה on the same words, not a challenge to the first one.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the meaning of what is written

phrases.english: Rava expounded: What is the meaning of that which is written:
'The mandrakes give off fragrance'?
phrases.notes: Here דודאים is read in its plain sense, fragrant mandrake plants.

phrases.english: These are the young men of Israel
who have not tasted the taste of sin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, independent דרשה on the same verse cited in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'הדודאים נתנו ריח' refers to young Jewish men who never tasted sin.

steps.title: The choice fruits at our doors are faithful Jewish wives
steps.stepSummary: רבא continues with the next part of the verse: 'at our doors are all choice fruits' refers to Jewish women who tell their husbands about their 'doorway,' meaning their status of נדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And at our doors are all choice fruits': these are the daughters of Israel who tell their husbands about their doorways.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the second half of the same verse and applies it to the modesty and honesty of Jewish wives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is a wordplay: מגדים ('choice fruits') sounds like מגידות ('they tell'), and פתחינו ('our doors') becomes פתחיהן ('their doorways'). The women tell their husbands when they are נדה so that the husbands do not come to sin.

keyTerms.meaning: our doors; read here as a modest reference to a woman's body
they tell, they inform (a wordplay on מגדים)

phrases.english: 'And at our doors are all choice fruits'
these are the daughters of Israel
who tell their husbands about their 'doorways.'
phrases.notes: They tell their husbands when they are נדה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's דרשה with the next clause of the same verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'At our doors are all choice fruits' refers to Jewish wives who tell their husbands about their נדה status (מגדים read as מגידות).

steps.title: A second version: wives who keep themselves only for their husbands
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the wordplay reads מגדים as אוגדות: the women 'bind,' or reserve, themselves only for their husbands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: they bind their doorways for their husbands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of רבא's explanation of the word מגדים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, מגדים is read as אוגדות ('they bind, they tie up') instead of מגידות ('they tell'). The praise is now about faithfulness: the women keep themselves only for their husbands and have no relations with anyone else. Both versions praise the צניעות of Jewish wives. They differ only in which wordplay is used.

keyTerms.meaning: they bind, they tie up (here: they reserve themselves)

steps.whatToRemember: The verse 'הדודאים נתנו ריח' is read in two ways. The first reading teaches that both צדיקים and רשעים will eventually be 'fragrant.' רבא's reading praises young men who never sinned and faithful wives. For the wives, the word מגדים is explained either as מגידות (they tell) or אוגדות (they bind).

phrases.english: Another version:
who bind their 'doorways' for their husbands.
phrases.notes: They keep themselves only for their husbands. מגדים is read as אוגדות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different wordplay for the same phrase explained in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the alternate version, מגדים is read as אוגדות: Jewish wives reserve themselves only for their husbands.

steps.title: New and old: Israel's extra decrees
steps.stepSummary: The end of the verse, 'new and old I stored away for You,' describes כנסת ישראל telling הקב"ה that it took on many decrees beyond what the Torah required, and kept them.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'New and old, my Beloved, I have stored away for You.' The Congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the World, I decreed many decrees upon myself, more than what You decreed upon me, and I kept them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps explaining the same verse from שיר השירים, now its last phrase. 'Old' is what הקב"ה commanded, and 'new' is the extra decrees Israel added on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 5-6 explained 'at our doors are all choice fruits' as praise of Jewish women. Now the rest of the verse becomes praise of all of כנסת ישראל: it did more than it was asked and actually kept the extra decrees. The 'new' fruits are the rabbinic additions to the 'old' Torah laws.

keyTerms.meaning: New and also old (here: new rabbinic decrees and old Torah laws)
The Congregation of Israel, the Jewish people as a whole

phrases.english: "New and also old
my Beloved, I have stored away for You"
The Congregation of Israel said
before the Holy One, blessed be He:
Master of the World,
I decreed many decrees upon myself
phrases.notes: He means rules made by the חכמים.

phrases.english: more than what You decreed upon me,
and I fulfilled them.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָשִׁים גַּם יְשָׁנִים דּוֹדִי צָפַנְתִּי לָךְ אָמְרָה כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the verse-by-verse reading of שיר השירים ז:יד, moving on to its final phrase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'New and old' means the rabbinic decrees Israel took on in addition to the Torah's laws, and Israel kept all of them.

steps.title: רב חסדא asks what 'new and old' means
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא asks a scholar who was reciting אגדה before him whether he had heard an explanation of 'new and old.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to one of the Rabbis who was arranging אגדה before him: Have you heard what 'new and old' means?
steps.whatsHappening: A short story starts here about the same phrase. רב חסדא tests a scholar by asking what 'new and old' means, which sets up the answer and discussion that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question asking for information, not an attack. It opens a short exchange that will end by agreeing with step 7: 'old' is Torah law and 'new' is rabbinic law.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, a sage of the גמרא period
Arranging and reciting אגדה traditions in order
Have you heard (a tradition about this)?

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said to
a certain one of the Rabbis
who was arranging aggadah before him:
Have you heard
what "new and also old" means?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שְׁמִיעַ לָךְ חֲדָשִׁים גַּם יְשָׁנִים מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story about how to read the same phrase explained in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do 'new' and 'old' in the verse refer to?

steps.title: The scholar: light and heavy מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The scholar answers that 'new and old' refers to light מצוות and severe מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: These are the light מצוות, and these are the severe מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholar gives his answer: the two words stand for two kinds of Torah מצוות, light ones and severe ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, both 'new' and 'old' are Torah מצוות, just sorted by how serious they are. The answer does not explain why light מצוות would be called 'new' and severe ones 'old,' and רב חסדא will attack exactly that point.

phrases.english: He said to him:
These are the light מצוות
and these are the severe מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵלּוּ מִצְוֹת קַלּוֹת וְאֵלּוּ מִצְוֹת חֲמוּרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's question from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'New' means light מצוות and 'old' means severe מצוות.

steps.title: Was the Torah given in separate batches?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא objects: calling some מצוות 'new' and others 'old' would mean the Torah was given at different times, and it was not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But was the Torah given on separate occasions?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא challenges the scholar's answer. 'New and old' implies things that came at different times, but all Torah מצוות, light and severe, were given together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is on the words 'new' and 'old,' which describe time, not severity. If both groups are Torah מצוות given at the same time at סיני, neither one is 'newer' than the other, so the scholar's reading does not fit the verse.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it so that...? (opens a rhetorical challenge)
At separate times, on several occasions

phrases.english: He said to him:
But was the Torah
given on separate occasions?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the scholar's answer in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'new and old' as light and severe מצוות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'New' and 'old' describe different times. All Torah מצוות were given together, so this split does not match the verse's words.

steps.title: Old is Torah law, new is rabbinic law
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא gives the correct reading: one group is דברי תורה (old) and the other is דברי סופרים (new).
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: these are from the words of the Torah, and these are from the words of the Sages.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the scholar's answer, רב חסדא gives his own explanation: 'old' means Torah laws and 'new' means laws the Rabbis added later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reading fits the time-words: Torah law came first at סיני and rabbinic decrees came later, so they really are 'old' and 'new.' It matches step 7, where Israel took on decrees beyond what הקב"ה commanded.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (rejects the earlier idea and offers a new one)

steps.whatToRemember: 'חדשים גם ישנים': ישנים = דברי תורה (given first), חדשים = דברי סופרים (added later by the Rabbis).

phrases.english: Rather —
these are from the words of the Torah,
phrases.notes: These are the 'old' ones.

phrases.english: and these are from the words of the Sages.
phrases.notes: These are the 'new' ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הַלָּלוּ מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְהַלָּלוּ מִדִּבְרֵי סוֹפְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reading that step 10 rejected with one that fits the words 'new' and 'old.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'New and old' means light and severe Torah מצוות.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Old' means Torah law and 'new' means rabbinic law, which really did come at different times.

steps.title: רבא: be more careful with rabbinic words
steps.stepSummary: רבא reads a verse in קהלת as teaching: my son, be more careful with דברי סופרים than with דברי תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא expounded: What does it mean when it is written, 'And more than these, my son, be careful; of making many books there is no end'? My son, be careful with the words of the Sages even more than with the words of the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a new verse on the same theme of rabbinic law. He reads 'more than these... books (ספרים)' as 'more than Torah law, be careful with the Sages (סופרים).'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse's word 'ספרים' (books) is read as 'סופרים' (the Sages), and 'more than these' becomes 'more than Torah law.' This goes further than step 11: rabbinic law is not only a real part of what Israel keeps, it calls for even more care.

keyTerms.meaning: What is meant by what is written?
Books, here read as סופרים, the Sages

phrases.english: Rava expounded:
What is meant by that which is written:
"And more than these, my son, be careful
of making many books, etc."
phrases.notes: קהלת יב:יב

phrases.english: My son, be careful with the words of the Sages
more than with the words of the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ רָבָא מַאי דִּכְתִיב וְיוֹתֵר מֵהֵמָּה בְּנִי הִזָּהֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the theme of דברי סופרים from step 11 with a new verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One must be even more careful with דברי סופרים than with דברי תורה.

steps.title: Why: breaking rabbinic law brings death
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives his reason: Torah law has positive and negative commandments with different punishments, but anyone who breaks דברי סופרים is חייב מיתה.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the words of the Torah contain positive commandments and negative commandments, but the words of the Sages: anyone who transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains why rabbinic law needs extra care. Many Torah laws carry lighter consequences, but breaking a rabbinic law makes a person חייב מיתה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Torah law is varied: some laws are עשה and many לאוים carry only lashes. רבא says breaking דברי סופרים carries the death penalty, which רש"י links to the verse 'ופורץ גדר ישכנו נחש' (one who breaks through a fence will be bitten by a snake). Breaking the Rabbis' 'fence' is treated as very serious.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable to death (here at the hands of Heaven)

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean a בית דין executes people for rabbinic laws, and it does not make rabbinic law stricter in every way (for example, ספק דרבנן לקולא). The 'death' is a punishment from Heaven. The point is how serious it is to break the Rabbis' protective fence.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא: be more careful with דברי סופרים than with דברי תורה, because whoever breaks דברי סופרים is חייב מיתה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is a main source for how seriously rabbinic law must be taken, even though in other ways (such as cases of doubt) it can be more lenient.

phrases.english: For the words of the Torah
contain positive and negative commandments.
phrases.notes: Many of these carry only lashes, or no punishment at all

phrases.english: But the words of the Sages —
anyone who transgresses the words of the Sages
is liable to death.
phrases.notes: Based on 'ופורץ גדר ישכנו נחש' (קהלת י:ח)

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה יֵשׁ בָּהֶן עֲשֵׂה וְלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רבא's claim in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Breaking דברי סופרים makes one חייב מיתה, so they need even more care than Torah laws, which include lighter categories.

steps.title: Why the words of the Sages were not written in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבא heads off an expected question: if דברי סופרים are so important, why weren't they written down? The verse answers that there would be no end to the books.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe you will ask: if the words of the Sages really matter, why weren't they written down? The verse says: 'Of making many books there is no end.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues his explanation of the verse in קהלת. He answers a question a listener might ask before the listener can ask it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think that if a teaching is not written in the Torah, it must be less important. רבא reads the next words of the verse to say the opposite. The Oral Torah is so huge that writing it all down would take endless books.

keyTerms.meaning: Lest you say. It introduces a question the speaker expects you to ask.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new speaker raising a challenge. It is still רבא, answering a question he expects in advance as part of the same teaching.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
If they (the words of the Sages) have substance,
why were they not written?!
The verse says:
"Of making many books there is no end."
phrases.notes: קהלת 12:12. The Oral Torah is endless and cannot all be written down.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר: אִם יֵשׁ בָּהֶן מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's reading of the verse in קהלת. It defends the importance of דברי סופרים against an expected objection.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דברי סופרים were not left unwritten because they lack weight. The Oral Torah is simply too vast to write down.

steps.title: Mocking the Sages brings a harsh punishment
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא, quoting רב אחא בר עולא, reads 'ולהג הרבה יגיעת בשר' as teaching that whoever mocks the words of the חכמים is punished with boiling excrement.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And much study is a weariness of the flesh.' רב פפא son of רב אחא בר אדא said in the name of רב אחא בר עולא: this teaches that anyone who mocks the words of the Sages is sentenced to boiling excrement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next phrase of the same verse. A new אמורא explains it as a warning against mocking the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא connects the word להג to the similar-sounding root לעג, which means to mock. He links 'weariness of the flesh' to a bodily punishment for someone who ridicules rabbinic teachings.

keyTerms.meaning: Study or deep thought (the word written in the verse)
Boiling excrement, a punishment in the next world

phrases.english: "And much study is a weariness of the flesh" —

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא
phrases.english: Rav Pappa, son of Rav Acha bar Adda, said
in the name of Rav Acha bar Ulla:
This teaches that anyone who mocks
the words of the Sages
is sentenced to boiling excrement.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְלַהַג הַרְבֵּה יְגִיעַת בָּשָׂר״ — אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the next phrase of the same verse in קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who mocks the words of the חכמים is punished with boiling excrement.

steps.title: רבא objects that the verse says להג, not לעג
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רב פפא's reading. The verse does not say לעג (mocking). It says להג.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: Does the verse say לעג (mocking)? It says להג!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the explanation from the previous step. He points to the exact word written in the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא's reading depends on treating להג as if it meant לעג. רבא says you cannot change the word. The verse is written with a ה, not an ע, so it is not talking about mocking.

phrases.english: Rava strongly objects to it:
Is it written 'la'ag' (mocking)?
'Lahag' is what is written!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא: מִי כְּתִיב לַעַג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading given in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's reading of להג as mocking
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The written word is להג, not לעג. A reading built on the meaning 'mock' does not fit the actual text.

steps.title: רבא's reading: studying the Sages' words tastes like meat
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives his own reading. Whoever thinks deeply about the words of the חכמים tastes the taste of meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: anyone who thinks deeply about them tastes the taste of meat.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected the first reading, רבא offers a new explanation of the verse that fits the word להג.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads להג as coming from הוגה, meaning to study or think deeply. He reads בשר as meat, not as the flesh of the body. So the verse turns from a warning into praise: learning דברי סופרים is as satisfying as eating meat.

keyTerms.meaning: One who studies or thinks deeply

steps.whatToRemember: The verse in קהלת is read as a positive lesson about דברי סופרים. Learning them is a real delight, like tasting meat.

phrases.english: Rather: anyone who thinks deeply about them
tastes the taste of meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading with one that matches the written word.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: להג means mocking, so the verse warns of punishment for mocking the חכמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: להג means deep study, and בשר means meat. Studying the words of the חכמים is as sweet as meat.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא in prison receives measured water
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא begins a story. רבי עקיבא was imprisoned, רבי יהושע הגרסי attended to him, and each day he was brought a measured amount of water.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: it once happened that רבי עקיבא was locked in prison, and רבי יהושע הגרסי served him. Every day they would bring him water in a measured amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story about how seriously רבי עקיבא kept דברי סופרים. This step only sets the scene. The point of the story comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail is that the water was limited to a set amount each day. This prepares for a moment when there is not enough water, and רבי עקיבא will have to choose how to use it.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
It once happened with Rabbi Akiva
that he was locked in prison,
and Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi would serve him.
Every single day
they would bring him water in a measured amount.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that illustrates how seriously דברי סופרים must be treated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup of the story: רבי עקיבא in prison had only a measured daily supply of water.

steps.title: The guard spills half of the water
steps.stepSummary: One day the prison guard saw that the water was more than usual. He suspected it would be used to dig through the prison walls, so he poured out half and let only half in.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day the prison guard met him. He said: your water today is a lot. Maybe you need it to dig through the prison? He poured out half of it and gave him half.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. Now רבי עקיבא will have only half his usual water, which sets up the test that comes next in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guard feared that the extra water would be used to soften the walls for tunneling out. Cutting the water in half creates the crisis. With so little water, רבי עקיבא must decide whether to drink it or use it for a rabbinic מצוה.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹם אֶחָד מְצָאוֹ שׁוֹמֵר בֵּית הָאֲסוּרִין,
phrases.english: One day the prison guard met him,
and said to him: Today your water is a lot,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא לַחְתּוֹר בֵּית הָאֲסוּרִין אַתָּה צָרִיךְ?
phrases.english: perhaps you need it to dig through the prison?
He poured out half of it
and gave him half.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹם אֶחָד מְצָאוֹ שׁוֹמֵר בֵּית הָאֲסוּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by creating the shortage of water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guard cut רבי עקיבא's water supply in half, which sets up the test of his commitment to דברי סופרים.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא notices the water is short
steps.stepSummary: When רבי יהושע הגרסי arrives with only half the water, רבי עקיבא tells him that he is old and that his life depends on him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came to רבי עקיבא, he said to him: יהושע, don't you know that I am old and my life depends on your life?
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. רבי עקיבא sees the small amount of water and gently tells רבי יהושע that his survival depends on him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע is the only one bringing water, so a shortage really endangers רבי עקיבא. This raises the stakes: the water is life-or-death, which makes his next request striking.

keyTerms.meaning: My life depends on your life

phrases.english: When he came to Rabbi Akiva,
he said to him: Yehoshua,
don't you know that I am old
phrases.notes: He saw that the water was less than usual.

phrases.english: and my life depends on your life?
phrases.notes: No one else brings him water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story right after the guard poured out half the water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: רבי עקיבא depends entirely on the water רבי יהושע brings.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא asks for water to wash his hands
steps.stepSummary: After hearing what happened, רבי עקיבא asks for the water for נטילת ידים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He told him the whole incident. He said to him: Give me water so that I can wash my hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע explains what the guard did. Surprisingly, רבי עקיבא's first request is to use the water for washing his hands, which sets up the next exchange.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even knowing there is only half the water, רבי עקיבא puts נטילת ידים first. This request is the setup for רבי יהושע's objection in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: So that I may wash my hands (נטילת ידים)

phrases.english: He told him that entire incident.
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע explains the guard poured out half.

phrases.english: He said to him: Give me water
so that I may wash my hands,
phrases.notes: Washing before eating bread.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the news of the shortage with an unexpected request.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא wants to use the limited water for נטילת ידים.

steps.title: There is not even enough to drink
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע objects: there isn't enough water to drink, so how can it be used for washing hands?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For drinking it's not enough, and for washing your hands it's enough?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע pushes back on רבי עקיבא's request. He argues that drinking to stay alive should come before washing hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like a challenge in the story: survival should beat a rabbinic rule. It sets up רבי עקיבא's answer about how serious the words of the חכמים are.

phrases.english: He said to him: For drinking they are not enough,
for washing your hands they are enough?!
phrases.notes: He's not really asking; he's pushing back.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִשְׁתּוֹת אֵין מַגִּיעִין, לִיטּוֹל יָדֶיךָ מַגִּיעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the request in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's request to use scarce water for נטילת ידים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Drinking keeps a person alive, so it should take priority over washing hands.

steps.title: Better to die than go against the Sages
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers that ignoring the words of the חכמים carries a death penalty, so he would rather die of thirst than violate their rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What can I do? For this one is liable to death. Better I die my own death than go against the opinion of my colleagues!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא answers רבי יהושע's objection. He explains that ignoring נטילת ידים is so serious that he would rather die of thirst.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words 'שחייבים עליהן מיתה' echo רבא's teaching in step 13, that anyone who transgresses דברי סופרים is חייב מיתה. Dying of thirst is 'his own death,' while breaking the rule of the חכמים is a sin that carries a death penalty, so he chooses thirst.

keyTerms.meaning: One is liable to death for them
My own death (by natural causes, here thirst)
The opinion of my colleagues (the חכמים who made the rule)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a practical ruling that one must risk his life for נטילת ידים. It is a story showing רבי עקיבא's extreme personal devotion to the words of the חכמים.

phrases.english: He said to him: What can I do
for one is liable to death for them?
phrases.notes: Eating without washing hands goes against the words of the חכמים.

phrases.english: Better that I die my own death,
phrases.notes: By thirst.

phrases.english: and not transgress the opinion of my colleagues!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Value priority: the seriousness of the words of the חכמים outweighs physical need
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Drinking to survive should come before a rabbinic washing rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: Breaking the words of the חכמים is a serious sin, while dying of thirst is not, so רבי עקיבא chooses to wash.

steps.title: He ate nothing until he washed
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא tasted nothing until water was brought and he washed his hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: He did not taste anything until he brought him water and he washed his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reports what happened next. רבי עקיבא actually kept his word and did not eat until he had washed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows his answer was not just words. He really acted on it, even though he was weak and thirsty.

phrases.english: They said: He did not taste anything

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁהֵבִיא לוֹ מַיִם וְנָטַל יָדָיו,
phrases.english: until he brought him water and he washed his hands,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reports that רבי עקיבא acted on his answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא refused to eat before נטילת ידים.

steps.title: The Sages draw a lesson from רבי עקיבא's behavior
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reason with two קל וחומר arguments: if he was this careful when old and in prison, he must have been even more careful when young and free.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the חכמים heard about it, they said: If in his old age he is like this, how much more so in his youth. And if in prison he is like this, how much more so when not in prison.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the reaction of the חכמים. They use two קל וחומר arguments to praise how careful רבי עקיבא always was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Old age and prison are the hardest conditions for keeping מצוות. If he was so strict even then, he surely was even stricter when he was young, strong, and free.

keyTerms.meaning: How much more so (a קל וחומר phrase)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא would rather risk dying of thirst than eat without נטילת ידים. This shows how seriously one must take the words of the חכמים.

phrases.english: When the Sages heard about the matter, they said:
If in his old age he is like this,
in his youth, how much more so.
And if in prison he is like this,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִין עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: when not in prison, how much more so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the moral from the story's ending.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי עקיבא's devotion to the words of the חכמים was total at every stage of his life.

steps.title: A בת קול praises שלמה
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל: when שלמה instituted עירובין and נטילת ידים, a בת קול praised him with a verse from משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: When שלמה instituted עירובין and נטילת ידים, a בת קול came out and said: 'My son, if your heart is wise, My heart will be glad, even Mine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching. It connects to the story about נטילת ידים and to our מסכת about עירובין, both of which were enacted by שלמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שלמה added protective rules around the Torah. Heaven itself shows approval of these rules, which fits the story just told about רבי עקיבא's devotion to נטילת ידים.

keyTerms.meaning: עירובי חצרות, the rule allowing carrying between shared courtyards on שבת

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that rabbinic safeguards like עירובין and נטילת ידים are praised by Heaven, tying the whole aggadah back to the topic of the מסכת.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
At the time that Solomon instituted
eiruvin and washing of hands,
a Heavenly Voice came out and said:
"My son, if your heart is wise,
phrases.notes: משלי כג:טו

phrases.english: My heart will be glad, even Mine."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story about נטילת ידים to the origin and praise of נטילת ידים and עירובין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה instituted עירובין and נטילת ידים, and Heaven praised him for it.

steps.title: A second verse of praise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second verse from משלי that also praises שלמה's wisdom.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it says: 'Be wise, my son, and make My heart glad, so that I may answer those who taunt Me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more verse to back up the praise of שלמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'ואומר' adds an additional verse. The second verse adds that שלמה's wisdom lets Heaven answer those who mock, showing these rules bring honor to Heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: And it says (introduces an additional verse)

phrases.english: And it says:
"Be wise, my son, and make My heart glad,
phrases.notes: משלי כז:יא

phrases.english: that I may answer those who taunt Me."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second verse supporting step 26.
steps.raayaObject: Heaven's praise of שלמה for enacting עירובין and נטילת ידים

steps.title: רבא quotes a verse from שיר השירים to expound
steps.stepSummary: רבא opens a דרשה by quoting the full verse from שיר השירים that he is about to explain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא taught: What is the meaning of the verse, "Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field; let us stay overnight in the villages. Let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine has flowered, if the grape blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom; there I will give my love to you"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new teaching. רבא quotes the whole verse first so he can explain it piece by piece in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase מאי דכתיב does not mean רבא is confused about the verse. It is the standard way to open a דרשה. Each image in the verse (field, villages, vineyards, vine, blossom, pomegranates) will be given its own meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught a homiletic explanation of a verse
What is the meaning of what is written (opens a דרשה)

steps.confusionAlert: מאי דכתיב is not a קשיא or a real question. It is just the opening formula for explaining a verse.

phrases.english: Rava expounded:
What is the meaning of that which is written
"Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field;
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 7:12

phrases.english: let us lodge in the villages.
Let us rise early to the vineyards;
let us see if the vine has flowered,
if the grape blossom has opened,
if the pomegranates are in flower;
there I will give my love to you."
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 7:13

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the verses praising שלמה (steps 26-27) to a new aggadic teaching by רבא on a different verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא will explain the verse in שיר השירים phrase by phrase.

steps.title: Do not judge us by the cities; see the scholars in the field
steps.stepSummary: כנסת ישראל asks הקדוש ברוך הוא not to judge her by the sinful city dwellers. She shows Him the תלמידי חכמים who learn Torah even in poverty and hardship.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field": כנסת ישראל said to הקדוש ברוך הוא, "Master of the world, do not judge me like the people of the big cities, where there is robbery, immorality, vain oaths and false oaths. Instead, 'let us go out to the field': come and I will show You תלמידי חכמים who learn Torah even though they are struggling."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the first phrase of the verse. "Going out to the field" means turning God's attention away from the corrupt cities and toward the hardworking scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city stands for sin: robbery, immorality, and lying oaths. The field stands for the simple scholars who work the land and still learn Torah, even with very little. כנסת ישראל is asking to be judged by her best people, not her worst.

keyTerms.meaning: The Congregation of Israel, the Jewish people as a whole

phrases.english: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field":
The Congregation of Israel said
before the Holy One, Blessed be He:
Master of the Universe,
do not judge me like those who live in large cities
where there is robbery and sexual immorality
and vain oaths and false oaths.
Rather, "let us go forth into the field":
come and I will show You Torah scholars
who engage in Torah study amid hardship.
phrases.notes: They work the fields and still learn, despite poverty.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״לְכָה דוֹדִי נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה״ — אָמְרָה כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first phrase of the verse quoted in step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The "field" is the place of the poor תלמידי חכמים, and Israel asks to be judged by them, not by the sinful cities.

steps.title: Read 'villages' as 'deniers': the ungrateful nations
steps.stepSummary: Using an אל תקרי reading, רבא turns כפרים (villages) into כופרים (deniers). Israel shows God the nations who received His goodness and still denied Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Let us stay overnight in the villages (כפרים)": Do not read it as כפרים, villages, but as כופרים, deniers. Come and I will show You the people You gave so much good to, and they denied You.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the second phrase by reading one word a little differently. Israel points to the ungrateful nations to show, by contrast, how loyal she is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אל תקרי does not change the written text. It adds a second layer of meaning from a similar-sounding word. The contrast is sharp: the nations got plenty and denied God, while Israel's scholars have little and still learn His Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read it as ... but as ... (a homiletic re-reading)
You showered or gave in abundance

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not mean the verse is spelled wrong or should be changed. The plain reading stays. The דרשה just adds another meaning.

phrases.english: "Let us lodge in the villages":
do not read it as "in the villages [bakefarim]"
but rather "by the deniers [bakoferim]":
come and I will show You those
whom You showered with good,
and yet they denied You.
phrases.notes: Refers to the nations of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues to the next phrase of the verse, using an אל תקרי re-reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The "villages" hint at the deniers: nations who received God's goodness and rejected Him.

steps.title: Vineyards and blossoms: the houses of learning and three levels of learners
steps.stepSummary: The vineyards are the בתי כנסיות and בתי מדרשות. The vine flowering, the blossom opening, and the pomegranates blooming match the three stages of learning: בעלי מקרא, בעלי משנה, and בעלי גמרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Let us rise early to the vineyards": these are the shuls and study halls. "Let us see if the vine has flowered": these are the people who know מקרא. "If the grape blossom has opened": these are the people who know משנה. "If the pomegranates are in bloom": these are the people who know גמרא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the rest of the plant images. Each stage of the plant's growth stands for a higher level of Torah learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order grows step by step: first the flower, then the opened blossom, then the full pomegranate. In the same way, a learner moves from מקרא (the verses), to משנה (the laws), to גמרא (the reasoning behind them). The pomegranate, full of seeds, fits גמרא, the fullest and richest level.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who are experts in the written Torah
Grape blossom, the early stage of the fruit
Those who are experts in משנה
Those who are experts in גמרא, the reasoning of the law

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the classic ladder of Torah study, מקרא, then משנה, then גמרא, with each level seen as a stage of the same growing plant.

phrases.english: "Let us rise early to the vineyards":
these are the synagogues and houses of study.
"Let us see if the vine has flowered":
these are the masters of Bible.
"If the grape blossom has opened":
these are the masters of Mishnah.
"If the pomegranates are in flower":
these are the masters of Gemara.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״נַשְׁכִּימָה לַכְּרָמִים״ — אֵלּוּ בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the ungrateful nations back to Israel's places of learning and its levels of scholars.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vineyards are the houses of learning, and the vine, blossom, and pomegranate are the levels of מקרא, משנה, and גמרא.

steps.title: There I will show You the glory of my children
steps.stepSummary: The final phrase means that כנסת ישראל will show הקדוש ברוך הוא her honor and greatness: the praise of her sons and daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: "There I will give my love to you": I will show You my honor and my greatness, the praise of my sons and my daughters.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the last phrase of the verse and finishes the דרשה. Israel's greatest gift to God is showing Him how good her children are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The "love" Israel gives is not an object. It is the pride of showing God her faithful sons and daughters. This closes the picture: instead of being judged by the sinners, Israel is judged by her loyal, learning children.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא reads the verse as כנסת ישראל's plea: do not judge us by the sinful cities. Look at the poor scholars, compare us to the ungrateful nations, visit our shuls and study halls, and see our learners of מקרא, משנה, and גמרא. That is our true glory.

phrases.english: "There I will give my love to you":
I will show You my glory and my greatness,
the praise of my sons and daughters.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שָׁם אֶתֵּן אֶת דּוֹדַי לָךְ״ — אַרְאֲךָ כְּבוֹדִי וְגוֹדְלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the last phrase of the verse and completes רבא's דרשה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Israel's true glory, which she offers to God, is the praise of her faithful sons and daughters.

steps.title: שלמה's thousands of parables and reasons
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא reads the verse about שלמה's 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs as referring to explanations he gave for every word of תורה and of דברי סופרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: What does the verse mean, 'And he spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs were a thousand and five'? It teaches that שלמה said three thousand parables on each and every word of the תורה, and one thousand and five reasons on each and every word of the סופרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about שלמה המלך, explaining a verse in מלכים that counts his proverbs and songs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the simple level, the verse just praises שלמה for writing many proverbs and songs. רב המנונא reads it as being about תורה: the 3,000 parables explain each word of the written תורה, and the 1,005 reasons explain each rule of the סופרים (the rabbinic laws). This shows how deep every single word of תורה is.

keyTerms.meaning: A parable or comparison used to explain an idea
Rabbinic teachings and enactments (literally, words of the scribes)
'It teaches', the word that opens the lesson drawn from a verse

steps.whyThisMatters: It ties into the larger theme of this part of the daf: rabbinic teachings are precious too, and שלמה himself gave reasons for them.

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"And he spoke three thousand proverbs,
phrases.notes: מלכים א ה:יב

phrases.english: and his songs were a thousand and five"?
It teaches that Solomon said

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל דָּבָר וְדָבָר שֶׁל תּוֹרָה
phrases.english: on each and every word of the Torah
three thousand parables,

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל דָּבָר וְדָבָר שֶׁל סוֹפְרִים
phrases.english: and on each and every word of the Scribes
one thousand and five reasons.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבא's דרשה on שיר השירים to a new teaching about שלמה's explanations of תורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה gave 3,000 parables for every word of תורה and 1,005 reasons for every word of the סופרים.

steps.title: קהלת taught with clear signs and comparisons
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes the verse in קהלת and explains that 'he taught the people knowledge' means שלמה taught with clear markers and explained each idea by comparing it to something similar.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא taught: What does the verse mean, 'And besides being wise, קהלת also taught the people knowledge, and he weighed, and searched, and arranged many proverbs'? 'He taught the people knowledge' means that he taught it with the signs of the טעמים, and he explained it with something similar to it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא quotes a full verse from קהלת and explains its first part. The second part of the verse is explained in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא says שלמה did two things to help people learn. First, he taught with the טעמים (the cantillation marks), which divide and clarify the verses. Second, he explained each idea through a comparison, which is what a משל does.

keyTerms.meaning: שלמה המלך, author of the book of קהלת
The signs of the cantillation marks. Some explain it as memory aids or signs.
With something similar to it, meaning by comparison

phrases.english: Rava taught: What is the meaning of that which is written:
"And besides being wise, Kohelet
phrases.notes: קהלת יב:ט

phrases.english: also taught the people knowledge;
and he weighed, and searched out,
and arranged many proverbs."
"He taught the people knowledge" means
that he taught it with the signs of the accents,
and he explained it through something similar to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues praising שלמה's teaching methods, now through a verse in קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה taught the people through clear signs and explained ideas by comparison.

steps.title: שלמה gave the תורה handles
steps.stepSummary: עולא in the name of רבי אליעזר reads אִיזֵּן as coming from אׇזְנַיִם (handles). Before שלמה, the תורה was like a basket with no handles, and he made handles for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he weighed, and searched, and arranged many proverbs': עולא said in the name of רבי אליעזר: At first the תורה was like a basket that has no handles, until שלמה came and made handles for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of the verse from the previous step. The word אִיזֵּן is read as 'he made handles.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אִיזֵּן sounds like אׇזְנַיִם, which means ears or handles. A basket without handles is hard to carry. Likewise, before שלמה the תורה was hard to grasp, and his parables and explanations gave people a way to 'hold onto' it and keep its laws.

keyTerms.meaning: He weighed. Here it is read as 'he made handles.'

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the תורה was lacking before שלמה. It means people found it hard to grasp, and שלמה's explanations made it easier to hold onto.

phrases.english: "And he weighed, and searched out, and arranged many proverbs":
Ulla said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
At first the Torah was
like a basket that has no handles,
until Solomon came
and made handles for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of the verse that רבא quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה's explanations gave the תורה 'handles,' so people could grasp it.

steps.title: Mounds of laws from every stroke
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא in the name of מר עוקבא reads קְווּצּוֹתָיו תַּלְתַּלִּים as teaching that piles upon piles of הלכות can be learned from every tiny stroke of the תורה's letters.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'His locks are wavy': רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא: This teaches that one can expound mounds upon mounds of הלכות from each and every thorn-like stroke of the letters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more praise of the תורה, a wordplay on a verse in שיר השירים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קְווּצּוֹתָיו (his locks of hair) is read as קוֹץ, the small thorn-like stroke on a letter. תַּלְתַּלִּים (wavy) is read as תִּילֵּי תִּילִּים, 'mounds upon mounds.' Together they teach that even the smallest mark in the תורה is a source for huge amounts of הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: His locks of hair, read here as related to קוֹץ
A thorn, meaning the small decorative stroke on a letter
Wavy or curly, read here as תִּילִּים
Mounds upon mounds, meaning huge amounts

steps.whatToRemember: This section praises the depth of תורה: שלמה gave countless parables and reasons for it and made it easy to grasp, and even every tiny stroke of its letters holds mounds of הלכות.

phrases.english: "His locks are wavy":
phrases.notes: שיר השירים ה:יא

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:

It teaches that one can expound

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mounds of הלכות can be expounded from every tiny stroke of the תורה's letters.

steps.title: Who truly holds on to Torah: reading 'black as a raven'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the last words of the verse, 'שחורות כעורב', and opens a question: in whom do you find the words of תורה? The answer begins with 'In him...' and continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Black as a raven': In whom do you find them (the words of תורה)? In him...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next explanation. It quotes the end of the verse, 'black as a raven,' and asks in whom words of תורה really stay. The answer is only starting here and finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 36 used 'קווצותיו תלתלים' to show how much הלכה comes from every stroke of the letters. Now the גמרא uses the next words, 'שחורות כעורב,' to describe the kind of person who keeps all that תורה. The question 'בְּמִי אַתָּה מוֹצְאָן' is not a real challenge. It is a teaching style that sets up the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Black (feminine plural). Here it describes the curls, or locks, in the verse.
In whom do you find them? This is a teaching formula that introduces a description of a certain type of person.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not treat 'בְּמִי אַתָּה מוֹצְאָן' as a קשיא. Nobody is objecting. It is a question the speaker asks so that he can answer it, and the sentence is cut off here in the middle.

phrases.english: 'Black as a raven':
phrases.notes: These are the last words of the same פסוק in שיר השירים (5:11) that was explained in step 36.

phrases.english: In whom do you find them (the words of Torah)? In him...
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the words of תורה. The answer breaks off here and finishes on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues reading the same verse. Step 36 explained 'קווצותיו תלתלים', and this step moves on to 'שחורות כעורב'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The words 'black as a raven' will be read as describing the kind of person in whom words of תורה are truly found. The full description finishes on the next amud.
